newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Close-up - Colston & Co.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Russell Barton's Canberra Close-up - Colston & Co.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)
It's cynicism on parade in Canberra -- a week that has underlined the notion that in the political race you should always back the horse called Self Interest.
Mal Colston might be the villain, but there aren't many on the stage who are not already, or are about to be, smeared with the odious substance that is being thrown about the parliament.
Senator Colston has not just become a man concerned with maximising his income and benefits.
It's long been a characteristic of the former long-time Labor stalwart from Queensland.
And the party has known of it all along.
But now he's a Labor defector, his vote in the Senate allows the government to push through its legislative programme.
The Howard government -- that administration which came to office on a platform of higher standards -- is so far prepared to shield Senator Colston from Labor's blowtorch to try to preserve his vote.
And even the man who puts himself above the political ruck, Tasmanian Senator Brian Harradine, finds himself with no option but to defend his "hard working" colleague.
Without Colston, Harradine loses his recently reacquired pivotal power to determine just what parts of the government's programme become law.

As an adjunct, that gives him also influence over just who the government appoints to key jobs, as we witnessed last week with Cabinet's decision not to proceed with the promised appointment of Professor John Funder to the National Health and Medical Research Council because of his apparent support for the "morning-after pill" RU 486.
But the buzzards are circling. Even the most cynical of the government's frontbench fear Colston can't be defended forever.
But the virulence of Labor's attack should be put in perspective.
For 22 years, the party has been pre-selecting Colston for the Senate.
In recent years it has been nominating him also for Senate committees, representations on the Australian National University's governing council and other perks carrying extra remuneration.
The rift between Colston and the party had its genesis in the final years of the Keating government.
Looking for new blood in the Senate the Labor machine sought to appoint Colston administrator of Norfolk Island, a post carrying a generous salary of over A$100,000 a year plus other entitlements.
But the senator decided he wanted to keep his parliamentary superannuation going while on the island, against regulations which stipulated it should be suspended for the duration of his appointment.
After a long wrangle, Colston refused to budge.
In the end the machine decided it was equally determined and the scheme was abandoned.
Colston then fought off all efforts to end his Senate career by removing his pre-selection.
After the election, Colston wanted to return to his old job of deputy president.
Labor wouldn't nominate him.
The government seized the opportunity to win his crucial vote and, against usual practice, nominated Colston itself.
Labor has not let too much time go by before wreaking its revenge.
Through a series of media leaks and questioning in Senate estimates committees, the party has begun exposing Colston's rorts and irregularities that it was quiet about for all those years.
On the other side, the government's dead-bat approach to the Colston revelations runs counter to its "higher standards" mantra.
And that's the reason the government will, in the end, be forced to plump for its standards above the Colston vote.
In the meantime the unfolding of the drama carries significant danger for both sides of politics.
Allegations of misconduct and misappropriation are OK if parties can be sure they are squeaky clean.
As recent events have shown, there can be no such guarantees.

Colston's affairs are now subject to deeper inquiry by the Administrative Affairs Department after initial investigation showed it was quite possible that Colston had breached regulations on his use of Commonwealth cars, often registering the use of his self-drive vehicle and the chauffeur-driven variety at the same time.
Similarly he's alleged to have claimed travel allowance for nights in Canberra when he was elsewhere.
But allegations have a way of spreading. Already two coalition MPs -- Senator Bob Woods and Michael Cobb -- are under Federal Police investigation over misuse of their entitlements.
Word around parliament is there's at least another two backbenchers under the microscope for similar irregularities.
Both of them are from the Labor party.
MPs entitlements are handed out on an honour system. There are no daily checks of their movements.
But some members and senators believe the extras are there to be plundered to make up for the low salary (just over A$80,000 a year for a backbencher).
The result is there could be many more rorters than revealed so far.
Many MPs therefore, are not enthusiastic about the Colston affair turning into an uncontrollable bushfire in which many of them could be badly burned.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
